A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoHAVE study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Material can be matched across the appendix reorganization and movement of computational-cost analysis into the main text.

before.justification: v1 reports original LRS3 and MuAViC experiments, routing analyses and ablations, including MoHAVE WER and BLEU results.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds DEMAND noise evaluation, multilingual hard-routing comparisons and language-wise routing analysis.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 retain the same decoder MoE, audio and visual expert groups, hierarchical routing, top-1 selection within each group, and load-balancing and load-biasing objectives. The additional experiments and notation clarification do not alter the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix D.1 adds LRS3 evaluation with recorded background noise from 18 DEMAND environments. This extends environmental-noise coverage within the existing AVSR task; the original datasets, multilingual recognition and translation tasks, and languages remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds mAV-HuBERT + Hard Routing to both noisy multilingual recognition and translation comparisons. These rows are absent from v1 Table 3, although hard routing was already evaluated on LRS3. Other existing comparator memberships are retained.

E3.justification: The added DEMAND evaluation samples SNR values randomly from −10 to 0 dB and reports WER by environment (v2 Table 6). Existing experiments retain their training schedules, model configurations, decoding procedures, metrics and noise settings; the relocated FLOP evaluation is unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds targeted environmental-noise robustness testing, language-by-layer expert-group analysis (Appendix C.2, Figure 7), and multilingual hard-routing controls. Existing expert-count, encoder-versus-decoder, uptraining, clean-condition and unimodal analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched existing result entries are unchanged. New multilingual hard-routing rows report average WER 39.3% and BLEU 16.8, versus MoHAVE's retained 37.4% and 19.5. New DEMAND results average 3.6% WER for MoHAVE-LARGE versus 4.1% for AV-HuBERT-LARGE, with two regressions and two ties. Figure 7 adds language-dependent routing observations.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes expert sets from their cardinalities in Equations 1, 3, 6 and 11. This clarifies equivalent notation without changing mathematical substance. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about efficient sparse scaling, adaptive modality-specific routing and strong noisy AVSR and multilingual performance. The additional evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.2 newly qualifies language-dependent routing by layer variation and the absence of explicit language-specific experts within groups. v2 also adds real-world applicability interpretations, speculation about EVA's competitiveness, and a word-level interpretation of unchanged WER differences. Existing limitations concerning clean and unimodal tasks remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents the DEMAND augmentation and SNR procedure and explicitly describes the shared AV-HuBERT-LARGE backbone and activated-parameter relationship of MIR-GAN, UniVPM and CMA. Existing training details remain; parameter breakdowns and FLOP measurement details are relocated rather than newly disclosed.

R1.justification: v2 adds the DEMAND citation and a focused Appendix B discussing previously cited AVMoE and EVA. It expands distinctions involving dense adapters, sparse experts and encoder-versus-decoder placement, and explains obstacles to direct comparison. Neither work becomes an evaluated baseline.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main narrative remain intact. Computational-cost discussion moves from v1 Appendix A.2 to v2 Section 5.2, supplementary material is reorganized into Appendices B–D, and localized explanations, acknowledgements and publication information are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 7 and the DEMAND results table, and expands the multilingual table with hard-routing rows. The computational-cost table moves into the main text with merged parameter columns. Existing tables receive highlighting and placement changes; Figures 1–6 retain their content.

improvement.justification: The multilingual hard-routing controls, DEMAND evaluation and language-wise routing diagnostics modestly strengthen empirical support beyond v1, while the relocated cost analysis improves accessibility. These benefits outweigh localized overinterpretation: Appendix B speculates about unevaluated EVA, Appendix D.1 overstates consistency despite regressions and ties, and Appendix A.2 infers word-level corrections from aggregate WER. The core method and previously reported results remain unchanged.
